To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the mean value of airborne trichloramines in indoor swimming pools was 0.65 mg/m3; (2) lifeguards and instructors experienced irritative symptoms more than other employees; (3) irritative symptoms become significant starting at airborne NCl3 level of >0.50 mg/m3.
lifeguards are at increased risk of developing ocular and upper airway irritation symptoms when airborne NCl3 concentrations are >0.5 mg/m3.
lifeguards, instructors and trainers are more exposed to airborne trichloramines than other swimming pool employees, and that they experience ocular and upper airway symptoms more frequently.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of the association between airborne NCl3 and self-reported health outcomes in indoor swimming pool employees.

the identification of the health risks associated with airborne NCl3 and the definition of an exposure level that is not associated with any health effect, which can be used as a reference value to define the occupational exposure limit.
the evaluation of the association between airborne NCl3 and irritative symptoms, with the aim of identifying the exposure level without health effects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
airborne NCl3 should be kept as low as reasonably possible, in particular for lifeguards and pool attendants, and that a value of 0.5 ppm should be considered the limit for health protection.
the WHO-recommendation of 0.5 ppm (0.5 mgl−1) is a good starting value for indoor swimming pool exposure control.
the risk of developing ocular and respiratory irritation is related to airborne NCh3 levels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the WHO-recommends value for airborne NCl3 (0.2 mg/m3) should be considered protective for lifeguards and swimming pool workers, and that a value of 0.5  mg/m3 could be considered a threshold for irritative symptoms.

airborne trichloramin is a risk factor of respiratory and eye irritative symptoms in indoor swimming pools, with a dose-response relationship, and that WHO-recommended levels are protective in the occupational exposure of indoor swimming pool employees.
the risk for respiratory symptoms in indoor swimming pools increases with increasing airborne NCl3 concentration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
airborne NCl3 is an irritant and its levels in indoor swimming pools must be carefully monitored.
there is a dose-response relationship between airborne NCl3 and the occurrence of ocular and upper airway symptoms.

it is possible to obtain detailed data on the dose-response relationships between airborne tricholoramine (NCl(3)) exposure and health effects in indoor swimming pool employees, and to identify the NCl(3) concentration level, if any without health effects.
